Without a proper understanding of reference electrodes, all electrochemical data becomes unreliable, and the bridge between laboratory science and real-world technology collapses.

We study reference electrodes because they are the indispensable, silent partners in any electrochemical measurement. They provide the stable foundation that allows us to:

  • Diagnose medical conditions with a blood test.
  • Prevent environmental disasters by monitoring pipeline corrosion.
  • Develop new batteries and materials in the lab.
  • Monitor our health with wearable technology.

1. Why do we need a stable reference electrode in electrochemical cells?

  • It provides a constant, known potential to measure the unknown potential of the working electrode.
  • Ensures accuracy and reproducibility in experiments like potentiometry and voltammetry.

Construction • Platinum wire coated with platinum black (to increase surface area) • Glass tube containing the electrode system • Hydrogen gas inlet at 1 atm pressure • Acid solution with 1M H+ concentration • Salt bridge connection to complete the circuit• Glass vessel with a side tube • Mercury at the bottom • Paste of mercury(I) chloride (calomel, Hg2Cl2) mixed with mercury • KCl solution of specific concentration • Porous junction for salt bridge connection• pH-sensitive glass membrane (composed of SiO2 with Na2O and CaO) • Internal reference electrode (usually Ag/AgCl) • Internal buffer solution (typically pH 7.0) • External reference electrode (also usually Ag/AgCl with KCl electrolyte) • Combined in a single unit for convenience
Working principle • Hydrogen gas is bubbled over the platinum electrode • Equilibrium established between H+ ions and H2 gas • Half-reaction: 2H+ + 2e- ⇌ H2 • Platinum acts as a catalyst for the reaction• Redox reaction: Hg2Cl2(s) + 2e- ⇌ 2Hg(l) + 2Cl-(aq) • Potential depends on Cl- concentration: E = E° - (0.0592/2) log[Cl-]2 • Mercury/mercury(I) chloride system maintains a stable potential Different Types: • Saturated calomel electrode (SCE): +0.2422V (most common) • 0.1N KCl: +0.3338V • 1N KCl: +0.2810V• Glass membrane develops a potential difference due to H+ ion exchange • Formation of a hydrated gel layer on the glass surface • Nernst equation for pH: E = constant - 0.0592 pH at 25°C • Measures the voltage difference between internal and external reference electrodes Mechanism of Ion Selectivity: • Glass membrane is selective for H+ ions due to specific glass structure • Silicate network with negatively charged oxygen sites • H+ ions exchange with Na+ ions in the glass • Selectivity depends on glass composition
Advantages • Highly reproducible under standard conditions • Reproducible with clean platinum and pure reagents; impurities can poison platinum • Platinum electrode is not consumed during the reaction• Stable and reproducible potential • Easy to set up and use • Portable for field measurements • Less sensitive to impurities than SHE• Single unit with both measuring and reference electrodes • Ease of use - no need for separate reference electrode • Compact and portable • Suitable for routine measurements • Compact, convenient, and minimizes errors as both sensing and reference systems are in one unit.
Limitations • Difficult to set up and maintain • Requires pure hydrogen gas at constant pressure • Not portable for routine measurements • Sensitive to temperature changes• Temperature sensitive (potential changes with temperature) • Contains toxic mercury (environmental and safety concerns) • KCl concentration can change due to evaporation • Not suitable for high- precision work• Used for measurements up to pH of 12. • Above pH 12 cations of the solution affect the glass interface & make the electrode useless.
Applications Fundamental science, the primary standard for all potential tables.Classic lab studies, corrosion testing, pH measurement & potentiometric titrationspH measurement in laboratories Industrial process control Environmental monitoring Biological systems (blood, urine analysis) Food and beverage industry

fixes.before_html:
Other gases and liquid-metal corrosion

• If Volume of the oxide is less than the volume of the parent metal- porous oxide layer (e.g. Li, Na, K & Mg).

2. Corrosion by other gases

  • Corrosion by gases like SO₂, Cl₂, H₂S, F₂, CO₂ etc
  • The extent of corrosion depends on the chemical affinity between metal and gas involved and the porosity of the film formed
  • If the film formed is non porous/protective then corrosion is limited to only external surface
  • Eg: AgCl film formed by attack of Cl₂ on Ag metal
  • If the film formed is porous or volatile then corrosion is deep
  • Eg: SnCl₄ formed by attack of Cl₂ on Sn metal

3) Liquid metal corrosion:

  • This is due to chemical action of flowing liquid metal at high temperatures on solid metal or alloy.
  • Such corrosion occur in devices used for nuclear power.
  • The corrosion reaction involves either:
  • (i) dissolution of a solid metal by a liquid metal or
  • (ii) internal penetration of the liquid metal into the solid metal.
  • Both these modes of corrosion cause weakening of the solid metal.
